name: Biotin
lead: Biotin, also called vitamin B7 or vitamin H, is a water-soluble B vitamin that serves as a cofactor for five human carboxylase enzymes involved in fatty acid, glucose and amino acid metabolism [1][2]. It is found in foods such as organ meats and egg yolks, and is sold as a dietary supplement alone or in multivitamins, commonly in doses of 1 to 10 mg marketed for hair and nail health [1].

Biotin deficiency is described as rare, and it can cause hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial skin rash [1]. Reviews of biotin for hair report that evidence in people with normal biotin status is limited: a 2017 review found 18 case reports of benefit, all in people with an underlying cause, and a 2024 review found three eligible studies, with the highest-quality placebo-controlled trial showing no difference from placebo [3][4].

Regulators and laboratory researchers have also documented that high-dose biotin can interfere with blood tests that use biotin-streptavidin technology, including thyroid and other hormone assays, producing falsely high or low results [1][5][6].
infobox: None set; adverse effects of high intake not determined [1]
500 to 1,000 micrograms daily without reported major toxicity (per a 2017 review) [22]

paras: Biotin is required for normal metabolism, and supplementation is the treatment for biotinidase deficiency and other genetic disorders of biotin handling, which can be fatal if untreated [1]. Newborn screening for biotinidase deficiency began in the United States in 1984 [1]. Large-dose biotin has been studied as a therapy for multiple sclerosis, and Wikipedia mentions 300 mg per day in that context [1][8].

Biotin is widely taken for hair, skin and nail quality, a use supported by its role in keratin-related metabolism and by the hair thinning seen in deficiency [1][4]. One randomised crossover trial in men compared 5% topical minoxidil, 5 mg oral biotin and the combination [9].

sections.h: Biotin and hair, skin and nails
paras: Biotin's appearance appeal rests on a straightforward chain: severe deficiency is known to cause thinning hair, brittle nails and a scaly facial rash, so supplementation is marketed as supporting keratin-rich tissues in people who want fuller hair, firmer nails and clearer skin.[1][22] Supplement doses in the milligram range are far above the roughly 30 microgram adequate intake.[1][22]

The 2017 review noted that biotin is inexpensive and widely added to hair and nail products, and that many people take 500 to 1,000 micrograms daily without reported major toxicity.[22] Acquired causes of low biotin that the review lists include raw egg white consumption (through avidin), certain medications, alcoholism, pregnancy, malabsorption and prolonged antibiotic use.[22]

The 2017 and 2024 reviews describe biotin as popular for hair while noting that no high-quality trial has tested it in healthy people.[4][22][23] Supporters in forum threads describe it as a cheap addition to a hair routine alongside treatments such as minoxidil, a pairing the 2024 crossover trial of minoxidil with biotin was designed to examine.[9][17]

The 2017 Skin Appendage Disorders review searched for case reports and randomised trials on biotin in hair, nail and skin conditions and found 18 reported cases of biotin use.[3][22] Every patient had an underlying problem with hair or nail growth and every one improved. Ten cases involved inherited deficiency of biotinidase or holocarboxylase synthetase, and eight of those had alopecia that resolved over several months of treatment. Other cases involved an infant with hair loss and skin inflammation on an amino-acid formula whose hair regrew after about two months, and a study linking valproic acid to lower biotin and biotinidase levels that improved after three months of supplementation.[22]

The same review describes three reported cases of uncombable hair syndrome whose hair quality improved after a few months of biotin, and three cases of brittle nail syndrome with improved nail strength and growth on biotin.[22] It found no randomised trials in healthy people, and noted that in a study of 541 women with hair complaints 38 percent had low biotin levels but only 11 percent had an identifiable cause, with seborrheic dermatitis common, leading the authors to regard hair loss as multifactorial. In laboratory culture, biotin did not change the growth or differentiation of normal follicular keratinocytes.[22] The authors concluded that evidence for supplementation in healthy individuals is limited, and that biotin may help in known congenital or acquired deficiency.[3][22]

The 2024 Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology review included three studies.[4][23] The highest-quality was a 1966 double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in women with diffuse hair loss in which 28 received biotin and 18 placebo for four weeks; both groups improved from baseline and the difference between them was not significant for hair growth or sebum production. In a 2021 unblinded study of 60 acne patients on isotretinoin, those who also took biotin for four months showed a shift toward growth-phase hairs on trichoscopy compared with baseline. In a 2021 study of women with self-reported hair loss after sleeve gastrectomy, subjective improvement was reported by 23 percent of biotin-deficient and 38 percent of biotin-sufficient participants, a non-significant difference.[23] The authors called for randomised trials in healthy people with self-perceived hair loss.[23]
A 2024 randomised crossover trial in men compared 5% topical minoxidil, 5 mg oral biotin and both together over hair growth outcomes.[9]

Studies of biotin interference with laboratory tests include a 2017 JAMA study of healthy adults,[6] a 2022 study of serum biotin interference in hormone immunoassays,[10] and registered studies of biotin supplementation and routine laboratory values.[11][12]

No upper intake limit has been set in the United States or by the European Food Safety Authority because adverse effects of high biotin intake have not been determined [1]. Absorption of supplemental biotin is described as non-saturable, with excess excreted in urine [1].

The principal documented concern is analytical. Intake of 5 mg per day or more can raise plasma levels enough to interfere unpredictably with biotin-streptavidin immunoassays used to measure thyroid hormones, vitamin D and other analytes [1]. A review noted potentially dangerous erroneous results in people consuming large amounts [13]. The JAMA 2017 study examined assay performance after biotin ingestion in healthy adults [6].

Biotin is attached by holocarboxylase synthetase to acetyl-CoA carboxylases 1 and 2, pyruvate carboxylase, methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase. It is also attached to histones, affecting chromatin structure and gene regulation [1][14]. Intestinal bacteria synthesise biotin, and dietary biotin is freed from protein by biotinidase [1].

Factors linked to higher requirement or lower levels include chronic alcohol use, some anticonvulsants, partial gastrectomy, and pregnancy and lactation; marginal deficiency has been reported in human pregnancy [1][13]. Raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin, according to Grokipedia [7].

US labeling reference values were revised in 2016 from 300 to 30 micrograms per day, with compliance required in 2020 to 2021 [1]. A review of the micronutrient literature is available from ESPEN [15]. Biotin is also used widely in biotechnology as a labelling and purification tag [1][16].

timeline.event: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial of biotin in women with diffuse hair loss finds no significant difference from placebo.[23]
US newborn screening for biotinidase deficiency begins [1].

lore.intro: Biotin is discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation as a hair supplement and, less often, as a debloating aid, with some users noting its effect on laboratory tests [17][19][20].

claims.claim: Biotin supports healthy hair and hair growth.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user says it is useful for healthy hair and hair growth despite others calling such supplements a 'cope', and a T Nation poster lists 12,000 mcg daily in his supplement routine [17][21].
claims.experts: A 2017 systematic review found improvement only in people with an underlying pathology and concluded evidence in healthy people is limited, and a 2024 review found a placebo-controlled study showing no difference in hair growth [3][4].

claims.claim: Biotin and collagen reduce bloating or water retention.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread relays a claim that a user with model-tier cheeks debloats with potassium, biotin and collagen; a reply says potassium debloats but biotin and collagen do not [17].
claims.experts: No studies of biotin and water retention exist.

claims.claim: High-dose biotin interferes with thyroid hormones.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says women take biotin for hair, skin and nails but that it seriously affects thyroid hormones and warns users to be careful [20].
claims.experts: Intake of 5 mg per day or more can interfere with biotin-streptavidin immunoassays used to measure thyroid hormones and other analytes, and a 2017 JAMA study examined assay performance after biotin ingestion [1][6]. The reviewed sources describe this as a laboratory-test effect.

claims.claim: Large amounts of raw egg whites can cause biotin deficiency.
claims.believers: T Nation posters discuss egg-white drinking and biotin absorption, with one saying he does not worry about it because the whites are pasteurized and another warning of deficiency with large raw amounts [18][19].
claims.experts: Grokipedia states that raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin [7].

claims.claim: Biotin is a cheap add-on to a hair routine alongside minoxidil.
claims.believers: Hair-focused users stack biotin with proven treatments as low-cost insurance for hair and nail quality.[17][21]
claims.experts: A 2024 randomised crossover trial compared 5% topical minoxidil, 5 mg oral biotin and both together in men; reviews find no high-quality placebo-controlled trial supporting biotin in healthy people.[4][9]

claims.claim: Biotin deficiency is common enough that most people with thin hair should take it.
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and some users treat low biotin as a routine cause of shedding and brittle nails.[22]
claims.experts: The 2017 review found 38 percent of 541 women with hair complaints had low biotin but only 11 percent had an identifiable cause, and describes deficiency as rare in the general population.[1][22]
